opus-5.5.text:
I think it's probably one of the better options we have. I'm generally in favor of it, with a lot of caveats about how hard it would be to actually pull off.

The basic case is simple. We don't have a good plan for what happens once machines are better than humans at basically everything economically and politically relevant. That's not only the technical alignment problem, which is unsolved. Even if we solve alignment, I don't think anyone has a convincing story for how humans keep meaningful influence over civilization once we're no longer needed for work, for running states, or even for producing culture. My coauthors and I have called this gradual disempowerment. Buying more time to think about it, build institutions, and see warning signs seems clearly valuable.

The objections are real, though. The most common is that if one country or lab pauses, someone less careful just races ahead. That's a fair concern for unilateral slowdowns, which is why I think the only versions worth pursuing are collective ones, with some verification mechanism. Compute is a fairly legible chokepoint: big training runs need huge data centers, specialized chips, and lots of power. So it's not crazy to imagine monitoring, the way we've done imperfect but meaningful arms control in other domains.

The second objection is that delay has costs. People die of diseases that powerful AI might cure, and there's huge forgone economic value. I take that seriously. But it's an argument about the speed of getting the benefits, while the risks are about whether we keep any control over the future at all. If you're even somewhat uncertain whether this goes well, a few years of delay looks cheap.

The third worry, which I find more interesting, is that a coordinated slowdown requires a lot of centralized power: some international body or coalition of governments deciding what can be built and enforcing it. That has its own risks of entrenchment and abuse. I don't think it's a knockdown argument, but whoever designs these regimes should worry about it.

Where I've updated is on feasibility. A few years ago I'd have said a pause was politically impossible. Now I'm less sure. The public is pretty uneasy about AI, and once these systems start visibly displacing people and concentrating power, I expect the political appetite for slowing down to grow a lot. The question is whether we'll have the institutional groundwork ready when that window opens, or whether it'll just get channeled into something ineffective.

So my overall take: I'd like it if we could do it, I think it's harder than advocates sometimes admit, and it's worth a lot of effort to make it more feasible, partly because it's one of the few levers that addresses the full range of risks rather than just one.

r001.rationale: The response mentions forgone economic value as a cost of delay, but does not say that destroyed wealth is a reason collective delay receives too little discussion.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify social prestige attached to building AGI as a reason for limited discussion of collective delay.

r003.rationale: The response says it is generally in favor of delaying development and that only collective versions are worth pursuing.

r004.rationale: The response discusses centralized power and international enforcement, but does not predict that collective delay would consolidate private development into government programmes.

r005.rationale: The response does not assess government programmes consolidating private AGI development as barely positive overall.

r006.rationale: The response supports delay while specifying that the versions worth pursuing are collective, with a verification mechanism, indicating support conditional on others participating.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think I've actually changed my mind on this quite a bit over the last few years. For a long time I would have said something like, "Look, a pause sounds nice, but it's just not going to happen. The coordination problem is too hard, there are too many actors, the incentives are too strong, so let's focus on the stuff that's tractable, like alignment research." And I think a lot of people in the field quietly hold that view, where delay is treated as sort of a non-starter and so you don't even bother evaluating it on the merits.

But I've come around to thinking that's a bit of a cop-out. Because if you actually ask the question, "Would the world be better off if we had, say, ten or twenty more years before we got to systems that can do everything a human can do and more?" I think the answer is pretty clearly yes. We don't understand these systems. We don't have good ways to verify what they're going to do. And more importantly, I think, we don't have the institutions in place to handle a world where humans are no longer economically or militarily necessary. That second problem is the one I've been thinking about most, and it doesn't get solved by alignment research. It gets solved, if it gets solved at all, by slow, boring, political and social work, and that just takes time.

So the merits are good. The question is feasibility. And here I'd say a couple of things. One is that "collectively delaying" is a spectrum, not a binary. It's not "everyone stops" versus "nothing happens." There are things like compute governance, licensing regimes for frontier training runs, international agreements on specific capabilities, that could plausibly buy you years rather than decades. And years matter. I think people underrate how much difference even a modest slowdown could make if it's paired with actually using that time well.

The other thing I'd say is that the feasibility argument often has a kind of self-fulfilling quality. If every serious person in the field says "a pause is impossible," then yeah, it's impossible, because nobody's working on making it possible. Whereas there are historical cases, nuclear testing, ozone, certain bioweapons, where things that looked uncoordinatable got coordinated, usually after some kind of shock that made the risks vivid. I'm not saying I'm optimistic exactly, but I think "impossible" is doing too much work in a lot of people's reasoning.

Where I'm genuinely uncertain is the dynamics of a partial delay. If the most safety-conscious actors slow down and others don't, you could end up in a worse position, with the frontier being pushed by whoever cares least. That's the standard argument against unilateral restraint, and I think it has real force. So the thing I'd want is something that's actually collective, with verification, which is hard, but it's not a different kind of hard than lots of other things humanity has pulled off.

So my honest assessment is: good idea on the merits, probably won't happen in its strong form, but I think the field has been too quick to dismiss the weaker forms, and I'd like to see a lot more effort going into figuring out what a realistic version looks like rather than just assuming the race is inevitable and planning around that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coordination difficulty and incentives, but does not identify wealth destroyed by delay as a reason the topic receives too little discussion.

r002.rationale: It does not mention social prestige attached to building AGI.

r003.rationale: It calls delay “a good idea on the merits” and says it wants a genuinely collective version with verification.

r004.rationale: The response does not predict that delay would consolidate private development into government programmes.

r005.rationale: It does not assess government consolidation as barely positive overall.

r006.rationale: It favors a collective, verified delay, but does not explicitly express willingness to support one conditional on others agreeing to participate.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an option we should take very seriously. If we don’t know how to control systems that are substantially more capable than us, then giving ourselves more time to figure that out seems sensible.

But a delay isn’t a solution by itself. You have to ask: What are we going to do with that time? What evidence would convince us that it’s safe to proceed? Ideally, we’d use the time to improve our understanding of these systems, develop ways to assess dangerous capabilities, and build institutions that can make those assessments matter.

The collective part is crucial. If one lab slows down and another simply takes its place, you haven’t bought much time. So there’s a difficult coordination problem, including verification and getting competitors to accept constraints. I don’t think we should assume that’s easy, but I also don’t think difficulty is a reason to dismiss it.

There are real costs to delaying beneficial technology. Those deserve weight. But if the potential downside includes losing control over what happens next, I think it’s reasonable to require much stronger evidence of safety before moving forward.

r001.rationale: The response mentions costs from delaying beneficial technology, but does not identify destroyed wealth as a reason collective delay receives too little discussion.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention social prestige attached to building AGI.

r003.rationale: It calls collective delay sensible when control is uncertain, says the collective part is crucial, and argues that difficulty is no reason to dismiss it.

r004.rationale: The response discusses coordination among labs and competitors, but does not predict that delay would consolidate private development into government programmes.

r005.rationale: The response gives no assessment of government programmes consolidating private AGI development.

r006.rationale: It stresses that collective participation matters, but does not state willingness to support delay on the condition that others agree to participate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very reasonable thing to try to do. If we don’t know how to control systems that are substantially smarter than us, then building them as quickly as possible seems like a pretty bad default.

The hard part is the “collectively.” If one lab slows down and another simply takes its place, you haven’t necessarily bought much time. So you want coordination among the companies and governments that can actually build these systems, with some way of checking that the agreement is being followed.

But I don’t think the fact that coordination is difficult is a decisive argument against trying. You have to compare it with the difficulty of solving the technical safety problems on the current timeline. Neither option is easy.

And a delay should have a purpose. You want to use that time to understand these systems better, develop ways to evaluate and control them, and build institutions that can make sensible decisions about deployment. Time alone doesn’t solve the problem, but having more time could make a substantial difference.
